lead: Two bedside monitors watch a rhythm. A foetal monitor separates the baby's heartbeat from the mother's and draws it against contractions. An arrhythmia monitor finds each QRS complex, measures the RR interval, converts it to rate, and alarms when the interval leaves set limits. Both are used in labour rooms, coronary care units and general wards. This chapter shows how each monitor separates the wanted signal from the unwanted one, and how a single missed beat can make a rate report look dangerously slow.
prereq: You need: 2.3 for heart sounds and phonocardiography, and ECG recording and the heart rate monitor (see Heart rate monitor, Holter monitor and ECG troubleshooting).

sections.h3: Foetal heart rate from the abdomen

blocks.text: The foetal heart is small and sits inside a moving mother. Two abdominal methods find its rate. An ultrasound Doppler transducer, usually 1 to 2.5 MHz, sends a continuous wave into the abdomen. Echoes from the moving foetal heart walls and valves come back shifted in frequency by f<sub>d</sub> = 2 f<sub>0</sub> v cos θ / c, where f<sub>0</sub> is the transmitted frequency, v the speed of the moving wall, θ the angle between beam and motion and c ≈ 1540 m/s in tissue. The shift is in the audible range, so the monitor can play it as a sound. The demodulated Doppler envelope repeats at the foetal heart rate; a band-pass filter removes slow maternal movement and fast noise.

Abdominal ECG uses electrodes on the mother's abdomen. The record contains maternal QRS complexes and foetal QRS complexes. The maternal complex is larger and regular. Subtraction estimates a maternal QRS template and subtracts it. Logic cancellation blanks the maternal QRS windows and keeps foetal peaks outside them. The cleaned signal gives foetal QRS times.

blocks.where: FHR is the foetal heart rate in beats per minute; T<sub>f</sub> is the time between two foetal beats in seconds. A rate of 140 beats per minute gives T<sub>f</sub> = 60/140 = 0.429 s.

items: Place the transducer or abdominal electrodes.
Record the mixed signal for several beats.
Mark maternal QRS complexes from the large regular peaks.
Cancel them by subtraction or logic gating.
Detect foetal peaks and measure T<sub>f</sub>.

sections.h3: Scalp electrode, contractions and the CTG trace

blocks.text: A direct foetal scalp electrode is a small clip placed on the foetal scalp after the membranes have ruptured and the cervix is dilated. It records the foetal ECG directly. There is no maternal QRS, so the signal is clean, but the method is invasive.

An intrauterine pressure catheter lies in the uterus and measures pressure. The cardiotocograph (CTG) prints foetal heart rate and uterine pressure together. The baseline is the average foetal rate over about 10 minutes, normally 110 to 160 beats per minute. Beat-to-beat variability is the small change from one foetal beat to the next, normally about 5 to 25 beats per minute. An acceleration is a brief rise. A deceleration is a fall.

blocks.text: Foetal phonocardiography uses a microphone on the abdomen. A filter selects the foetal heart sound band and rejects maternal sounds. It is passive and simple, but noise from mother and labour ward limits it.

An arrhythmia monitor watches one ECG lead. A QRS detector first removes baseline drift and T waves with a band-pass filter, often around 5 to 15 Hz. It then finds sharp peaks. For each beat it measures the RR interval, the time from one R wave to the next.

blocks.where: R<sub>inst</sub> is the instantaneous heart rate in beats per minute; RR is the interval between two adjacent R waves in seconds.

blocks.text: A monitor stores limits. Typical adult settings are tachycardia above 100 to 120 beats per minute, bradycardia below 50 to 60 beats per minute, and a pause when RR exceeds 1.5 to 2 s. Asystole is no QRS for a longer set time. The comparator drives an audible alarm and a message.

Artefact rejection checks QRS shape, a refractory period and the previous RR; a very short RR after a normal beat may be noise. Ectopic beats are flagged by timing and shape: a premature ventricular contraction comes early (for example at less than 80 % of the running RR average), has a wide QRS of 0.12 s or more, and is followed by a compensatory pause. A missed beat is the dangerous error. If the true RR is 800 ms and one QRS is missed, the measured RR becomes 1600 ms and the reported rate is 60/1.60 = 37.5 beats per minute instead of 75.
Figure 2.4.1 draws this: the bars are 800, 800, 1600 and 800 ms, and only the 1600 ms bar crosses a 1500 ms pause limit. One missed beat doubles one interval and halves the rate reported for it.

figure.caption: When the detector misses one QRS, the interval it measures is 1600 ms instead of 800 ms. That bar crosses the 1.5 s pause limit and the rate drops from 75 to 37.5 per minute, though the heart never slowed.

examples.question: A cardiotocograph on a mother at 38 weeks shows a baseline foetal heart rate of 140 beats per minute with variability of 5 beats per minute (the lower end of the normal 5 to 25 range). After one contraction the rate falls to 90 beats per minute; the fall starts 20 s after the contraction begins and its lowest point comes 30 s after the contraction peak. (a) Name the deceleration and its usual cause. (b) How long is one foetal beat interval at baseline? (c) In another ward an adult arrhythmia monitor with a 1.5 s pause limit measures RR = 1.60 s. What rate does it report, and which alarm sounds?
steps: (a) The fall starts after the contraction has begun and its lowest point lags the contraction peak, so it is a late deceleration. Late decelerations point to poor placental blood flow.
(c) Rate = 60/1.60 = 37.5 beats per minute. 1.60 s is longer than the 1.5 s limit, so the pause alarm sounds; check the strip for a missed QRS before treating it as a true pause.
examples.answer: (a) Late deceleration (placental insufficiency). (b) About 429 ms. (c) 37.5 beats per minute; the pause alarm sounds.

examples.question: A 2.0 MHz foetal Doppler probe looks straight along the motion of a foetal heart wall moving at 0.15 m/s (c = 1540 m/s). (a) Find the Doppler shift. (b) What shift does the same wall give if the beam meets its motion at 60°?
steps: Both shifts are audible, which is why the monitor can play the foetal heart as a sound; a poorly aimed probe gives a weaker, lower shift and the rate counter may drop beats.

traps: A large regular QRS at about 70 to 90 beats per minute on an abdominal ECG is often the mother's. Do not read it as foetal. Foetal rate is 110 to 160 beats per minute and needs maternal QRS cancellation.
One missed foetal beat doubles one RR interval and halves the rate calculated from that interval. The monitor is not measuring a true bradycardia.

Early deceleration starts with the contraction; late begins after the contraction starts, with its nadir after the peak; variable is abrupt and changes shape. The examiner often gives the timing and asks for the name.
Baseline rate and beat-to-beat variability are different. A baseline of 140 beats per minute can still have reduced variability, which is a warning sign.
Pause is one long RR interval; bradycardia is a sustained low rate over several beats. Check whether the alarm limit is in seconds or beats per minute.

quiz.q: What is the normal baseline foetal heart rate range on a cardiotocograph?
What measurement does an arrhythmia monitor take, and what relation converts it to rate?
quiz.a: The RR interval in seconds, converted by rate = 60/RR.

quiz.q: Why does abdominal foetal ECG need maternal QRS cancellation?
quiz.a: The maternal QRS is larger and mixed with the foetal signal. Cancellation by subtraction or logic reveals the foetal QRS peaks.

quiz.q: Why does a missed QRS halve the rate computed from one interval?
quiz.a: The measured RR doubles. Then rate = 60/(2RR) = half the true rate.

quiz.q: A foetal RR interval is 0.375 s. Find the foetal heart rate.
quiz.a: Rate = 60/0.375 = 160 beats per minute, the top of the normal 110 to 160 range.

quiz.q: An arrhythmia monitor records RR = 1.8 s. Find the rate and say which limit is crossed if the pause limit is 1.5 s.
quiz.a: Rate = 60/1.8 = 33.3 beats per minute. The interval 1.8 s is greater than 1.5 s, so the pause alarm is crossed.

quiz.q: A CTG shows baseline 145 beats per minute, variability 2 beats per minute, and a late fall to 100 beats per minute after a contraction. Interpret the trace.
quiz.a: Reduced variability plus a late deceleration suggests poor placental blood flow and possible foetal hypoxia. The trace needs clinical review.

beyond: Not for the exam. Home foetal Doppler devices use the same Doppler shift but no uterine pressure channel. Wearable ECG patches send RR intervals to a phone. Research improves maternal ECG cancellation with adaptive filters and machine learning. Search for non-invasive foetal ECG, CTG interpretation, and RR interval variability.
